list.listitem: The USPSTF recommends that clinicians screen all women of childbearing age for IPV, and refer women who screen positive for appropriate services. Evidence regarding screening in other groups with no signs or symptoms of abuse was insufficient.B
IPV is a common public health issue with both direct and indirect impact on the victims, perpetrators and witnesses and can cause health concerns, economic hardship and even lead to homicide. B

Suspect IPV in patients presenting with an inadequate or irregular history pattern, partner refusal to allow patient to be alone with provider, chronic or recurrent somatic symptoms, sleep disturbance, depression, or symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder. C
Clinicians have a professional and legal obligation to follow up on clinical suspicions of IPV.C
Recommend multidisiplinary appropriate responses (medical, community advocacy, legal, mental health, and criminal justice) depending on state laws and patient preferences.C

Intimate partner violence (IPV): IPV is an abusive behavior by someone who may be a current or former spouse or partner who wishes to be involved in an intimate or dating relationship with an adult or adolescent intimate partner or ex-partner that causes physical violence, sexual or psychological harm, physical aggression, sexual coercion, psychological abuse and controlling behaviors.

Intimate partner: include current and former spouses (including common-law spouses, divorced or separated spouses) as well as current and former marital or non-marital partners (dating partners, boyfriends/girlfriends). The United Nations defines violence against women as "any act of gender-based violence that results in, or is likely to result in, physical, sexual, or mental harm or suffering to women, including threats of such acts, coercion or arbitrary deprivation of liberty, whether occurring in public or in private life".

Physical violence (PV): The intentional threat or use of physical force with the potential for causing death, disability, injury, or harm by pushing, hitting, slapping, kicking, use of a weapon, and so on.

Domestic violence (DV): DV is defined as physical, sexual, emotional, economic, social, or psychological abuse against an intimate partner, child, or other relative. It affects many men, women, and children in a pattern of assaultive and coercive behaviors like progressive social isolation, stalking, deprivation, intimidation, and threats.

Sexual violence (SV): Any sexual act, attempt to obtain a sexual act, or other act directed against a person’s sexuality against his or her will, using coercion, by any person regardless of their relationship to the victim, in any setting. or sexual acts involving a person who is unable to understand the nature of the act.
Psychological/emotional abuse: Verbal and Non-verbal communication acts, threats of acts, or coercive tactics with intent to harm emotionally or mentally or to exert control over a partner.

Elder abuse or vulnerable adults: Types of abuse that apply to older or vulnerable adults include physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional or psychological abuse, neglect, abandonment, and financial or material exploitation.

Globally the lifetime prevalence of IPV is 26% among women and 0.9% among men (raped and or physically assaulted by a current or former partner). As per WHO the regional median prevalence is: African region 35%, South east Asian region 31%, Eastern Mediteranean region 30%, South Americas region 30%, Europeans region: 25%, Western Pacific region 18%.

US IPV: Millions are affected annually (1.5 million women and 834,700 men are raped and/or physically assaulted in other ways by an intimate partne), and it may start early in childhood. Adoloscent IPV (also called teen dating violence) has been reported before age 18 among 16 million women and 11 million men in their lifetime.
Over 61 million women and 53 million men have experienced psychological aggression such as humiliating or controlling behaviors by an intimate partner in their lifetime.

CDC data states that about 41% of women and 26% of men experienced IPV, either contact sexual violence (women 16% vs men 7%), physical violence (women 25% vs men 14%), or stalking (women 10% vs men 2%) by an intimate partner during their lifetime.

A study that looked at IPV during the COVID-19 pandemic outbreak in various countries discovered a 12-75% increase. The constant contact between perpetrators and victims due to confinement is thought to have resulted in increased violence. Reporting was also decreased due to workplace closures. School closures and online classes may have contributed to a decrease in child abuse reports by isolating students at home.

A systematic review of 11 databases and a meta-analysis of 25 studies found the 12-month prevalence of IPV among infertile women was 36% and a lifetime prevalence of IPV among women of low-income and middle-income countries was 47%.
A systematic review of 84 studies found that transgender individuals experience a higher risk of IPV than cisgender individuals (RR 1.7, 95% CI 1.4-2.0) and sexual IPV (RR 2.5, 95% CI 1.6-3.7).
In primary care settings 12% to 23% of women and in the ED 14% to 35% of women reported being physically abused or threatened by their partner within the last year.

Arab countries: Although data are limited, meta-analysis of pooled prevalence of IPV in Arab countries in 2019 was estimated to be lifetime exposure of 73% including 36% physical IPV, 22% sexual IPV and 50% emotional or psychological IPV.
Potential consequences of intimate partner violence are summarized in .
Common mental health outcomes reported in a meta analysis were depression (70%), suicidality (31%), post traumatic stress disorder (29%), and anxiety (17%).
A systematic review of 17 observational studies found an association between IPV and an increased risk of perinatal death (aOR 3.2, 95% CI 1.9-5.4).
A systematic review of 50 studies found an association between IPV and preterm birth, miscarriage, and perinatal death.

Intimate partner homicide (IPH): Secondary to IPV, a meta-analysis found that significant risk factors for female IPH victimization included lower education, separation, substance abuse, and having a child from a previous relationship.

Victims with (ex)partners who owned guns experienced increased coercive control and physical violence, stalking for a longer period of time, and more threats during the relationship. In a domestic violence situation, the presence of a gun increases the risk of homicide by 500%.
In Australia, the total annual cost of violence against women and their children was estimated to be $26 billion (2015–16), with victim-survivors bearing approximately 50 per cent of that cost.
Cycles of violence, which are learned behaviors by perpetrators who were victims themselves or who witnessed domestic violence.
Lack of parenting skills (young parents, lower educational status), and lack of knowledge regarding child development.
Unresolved traumatic events in the life of the parents/caregivers that contribute to the intergenerational transmission of abuse/neglect.

Societal and cultural acceptance of corporal punishment; social and economic stressors (eg, poverty, domestic violence, mental health issues, inadequate support systems, substance abuse, chronic illness, divorce, single parents); social pathology and criminal behaviors.

The COVID-19 pandemic caused social isolation, increased exposure to economic and psychological stressors, an increase in negative coping mechanisms (such as alcohol misuse) and an inability to access usual support mechanisms or escape abusive households owing to quarantine measures or travel restrictions.
Child abuse, neglect, parental conflict, parental mental health, and parental substance abuse issues; gambling, alcohol and drug use..
Prior history of domestic violence and witnessing or experiencing violence as a child.
Female gender, young (reproductive age), pregnant, lower educational status, lower socioeconomic status, infertile and gender identity disorder; sexual minority and controlling behaviors.

Individual (victim) Risk factors: The median odds ratios of the association of risk factors and IPV a the individual level include: previous violence victimization (OR 2.2), low education (1.8), history of child maltreatment (2.0), poor relationship skills (2.7), substance abuse (1.8), LGBT (Lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender) 2.0, mental and neurological disorder (2.5), unplanned or unwanted pregnancy (2.0), unmarried/single (2.6), HIV positive( 2.4), previous perpetration of violence (2.1), large size family (2.5), and witnessing IPV in childhood (2.1).

Individual (perpetrator) risk factors: The median odds ratios of the association of risk factors and being a perfpetrator of IPV include ethnic minority (4.1), gambling (3.0), unplanned pregnancy (2.8), anger (2.7), poor relationship skills (2.2), substance abuse (2.5), history of child maltreatment (2.0), and attitudes supportive of violence (2.3%).

Relationship risk factors: Dominance and control by one partner (2.3), marital dissatisfaction (3.0), married or cohabiting (2.0), marital conflict (2.5), low social support (1.3) child marriage (1.6), educational disparity (1.5).

The USPSTF recommends that clinicians screen all women of childbearing age for IPV, and refer women who screen positive for appropriate services. Evidence regarding screening in other groups with no signs or symptoms of abuse was insufficient.B

Interventions in adolescents have been shown to improve behaviors and reduce perpetration of IPV. B Early interventions in childhood reduce the risk of psychopathology and crime in adulthood (NNT = 8 based on an RCT with 9594 kindergartners). B

The USPSTF also found insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of primary care interventions to prevent maltreatment in children and adolescents without signs or symptoms of, or known exposure to, maltreatment (I statement). The task force recognizes the potential harms associated with biases in identification of child maltreatment may disproportionately disadvantage Black, Hispanic, and Native American/Alaska Native families.

A Cochrane review concluded based on 13 trials with nearly 15,000 women that screening increases the identification of women experiencing IPV, but relatively little evidence regarding the impact of screening on other health outcomes. B
summarizes strategies for preventing IPV. B
summarizes strategies for preventing IPV. B
HRSA provides training for the health care and public health workforce to address IPV along with an IPV Health Partner Toolkit.

The "Me and You" dating violence prevention program was found in a cluster randomized trial of early adolescent youths to reduce the odds of IPV perpetration (aOR 0.46, 95% CI 0.28-0.74) but not of IPV victimization.
Early interventions in childhood reduce the risk of psychopathology and crime in adulthood (NNT = 8 based on an RCT with 9594 kindergartners).

A cluster randomized trial of 973 middle school male athletes in 38 clusters reported that an athletic coach delivered program to reduce relationship abuse and sexual violence was effective, increasing positive bystander behaviors and recognition of abuse, while decreasing self-reported perpetration of abuse.
The USPSTF recommends that clinicians screen all women of childbearing age for IPV, and refer women who screen positive for appropriate services.

USPSTF found insufficient evidence regarding the balance of benefits and harms regarding screening of elderly or vulnerable adults for abuse and neglect. The USPSTF found no valid, reliable screening tools in the primary care setting to identify IPV in men without recognized signs and symptoms of abuse. The USPSTF found no evidence on appropriate intervals for screening.
A clinical prediction rule with 5 items has been validated as a screening tool for IPV in women in the emergency department.

Several screening instruments can accurately screen adult women for IPV within the the past year. The HARK has 4 items (Humiliation, Afraid, Rape, Kick). In a study of 232 women in a London general practice, a cutoff of >= 1 positive response was 81% sensitive and 95% specific (LR+ 16, LR- 0.19).
shows a simple 3 item screener that has been validated in the ED.

A noninterruptive electronic health record (EHR) alert developed by South Carolina researchers to screen for IPV was significantly more effective than traditional methods in identifying victims of IPV in an RCT.

However, a randomized controlled trial of computerized screening for partner violence did not find significant differences in quality-of-life, number of days lost from work or housekeeping, hospitalizations, emergency department or clinic visits, use of partner violence resources, or recurrence of partner violence.

The 15 item "ED Senior AID" screening tool was found to have good accuracy in a prospective validation study. Among 916 enrolled, 33 (3.6%) screened positive, of whom 16 were confirmed to have elder abuse (positive predictive value 48%, sensitivity 94% and specificity 84%).

A Cochrane review concluded based on 13 trials cumulative 15,000 women that screening increases the identification of women experiencing IPV, with little evidence regarding the impact of screening on other health outcomes.
A Cochrane review found no RCT evidence to support or refute screening for IPV in adults with facial or dental injuries.
History and physical examination are essential components to determine the diagnosis of domestic violence. C
Look for inconsistencies or red flags in either history or the physical examination (). B
Develop indirect approaches and identify questions that foster patient trust. C
Recommend interviewing the patient without the presence of the partner. C

Take a nonjudgmental approach and use open-ended questions. summarizes key red flags and their differential diagnosis. is a screening instrument validated in the emergency department; it is 71% sensitive and 84% specific.
A clinical prediction rule with 5 items has been validated as a screening tool for IPV in women in the emergency department.
The patient should be interviewed without the partner present at some point during the encounter.

Experts report a sudden realization of the diagnosis when a constellation of symptoms is observed, especially a history of previous abuse, anxiety, chronic headache, vague, chronic pelvic or stomach pain, or other GI symptoms.
Histories that are inadequate, have irregularities, or are unlikely with regard to the mechanism of injury suggest abuse, as does partner refusal to allow patient to be alone with the provider.

Physical symptoms suggestive of abuse include chronic pain, including headache, chest pain, abdominal and/or pelvic pain, chronic gastrointestinal complaints, irritable bowel syndrome, back and joint pains, chronic fatigue, noncompliance with medical treatment, frequently missed appointments, late appointments, and multiple previous visits to emergency departments.

Psychological symptoms suggestive of abuse include sleep disturbances, depression, suicidal ideation, posttraumatic stress disorder, anxiety syndromes, panic disorder, somatoform disorders, substance abuse, including tobacco, and eating disorders.
Behavioral indicators of abuse include evasiveness during history taking and physical examination, reluctance to speak in partner’s presence, overly attentive or outwardly abusive partner.
Assess the patient’s general appearance and the interpersonal dynamics between patient and the partner.

Assess the characteristics of injury. Look for suggestive patterns or types of injuries (eg, cigarette burns), multiple injuries (especially if at different stages of healing), injuries that do not match the history, or abnormal interactions with the partner (eg, observed fear of partner). Physical findings of any injury to face, head, neck, throat, abdomen, extremities, genitals, central distribution of injury (ie, areas covered by clothing), bruises, burns, broken bones, dental trauma, signs of sexual assault, defensive injuries of forearms, or sexually transmitted diseases including HIV/AIDS are all associated with an increased risk of domestic violence.
One study found that women preferred a self-administered screening tool to one that was administered in person by the physician.

Positive and trusting relationship with the healthcare provider was identified as an important facilitator for victims' disclosure. A study also identified social consequences of abusive behaviors, feeling heard by healthcare professionals, and emotional and practical support for relationship problems offered by healthcare staff as facilitators of disclosure.

Barriers to disclosure include: fear of having their children taken away, being judged or negatively evaluated by the healthcare provider or environment (such as family, friends, or neighbors), fear of the abuser, and a lack of trust in the ability of healthcare services to address domestic violence abuse.

Check blood counts(CBC), urinalysis(UA), coagulopathy panel (PTT/INR), serum chemistry panel, electrolyte panel (combined metabolic panel) in the patient with abdominal/pelvic trauma, fractures of unknown etiology, or dehydration.

Obtain drug testing in the patient with suspected poisoning or ingestions; and pregnacy testing for all females. Test for sexually transmitted disease and pregnancy if history or examination is suggestive of sexual abuse.

Obtain plain radiographs of suspected fractures (eg, point tenderness, bruising, or swelling over bony distributions) and CT or MRI for patients with suspected abdominal trauma, head trauma, or abnormal neurologic findings.
In general, evidence for interventions is lacking. B
Stabilization of acute medical and mental health consequences of DV should be offered. C
Long-term management includes assurance of safety and treatment of the victim, as well as treatment and intervention for the perpetrator(s). C
Appropriate responses should be multidisciplinary (medical, community advocacy, legal, mental health, and criminal justice), depending on state laws and patient preferences. C
Psychological therapies decrease depressive symptoms and anxiety symptoms, but it is unclear whether they improve self-efficacy, PTSD, re-exposure to IPV, or safety planning. B.
Providers should express concern for the patient’s safety and well-being and the discussion should be patient focused and nonaccusatory. C

When legal protection orders were used in conjunction with arrests, the rate of violation was reduced. Protection order violations were lower among perpetrators who had no history of being arrested for committing violence, perpetrators who did not engage in stalking, and couples with medium to high incomes.
Appropriate medications for the management of acute physical and mental health consequences of DV should be considered such as: treatment of pain, depression, anxiety, and infection.
Also consider prophylactic treatment for sexually transitted infections and provide emergency contraception for patients reporting sexual assault.

Adolescent girls experiencing sexual abuse–related PTSD benefit significantly more from prolonged exposure-based therapy than from standard supportive counseling (ie, more girls in the exposure-based therapy group were classified as good responders on a standard symptom scoring tool at 12 months).

Psychological therapies improve depression and anxiety symptoms, but it is unclear if a woman's ongoing needs for safety, PTSD symptoms, re-exposure to IPV, or safety planning support are improved. There is a need for more interventions focused on trauma approaches. No harmful effects were identified.

Trained healthcare and other workers who offer and deliver psychological therapies to women who have experienced any form of IPV may alleviate depression and anxiety symptoms. In terms of depression outcome, five or more sessions may be more beneficial than fewer sessions.
Mandatory reporting of IPV varies by state; providers should review local statutes as they pertain to reporting incidents of IPV.

Hospitalization is indicated for acute stabilization of medical and mental health consequences of child abuse or neglect and if there are imminent safety concerns or significant delays in awaiting legal protection.

When legal protection orders were used in conjunction with arrests, the rate of violation was reduced. Protection order violations were lower among perpetrators who had no history of being arrested for committing violence, perpetrators who did not engage in stalking, and couples with medium to high incomes.
Multidisciplinary treatment (medical, community advocacy, legal, mental health, and criminal justice, depending on state laws and patient preferences) is recommended.
Cognitive behavioral therapy for perpetrators is of uncertain benefit, but it may be helpful for pregnant women in reducing recurrent violence.

Injury-specific management of acute and chronic medical consequences of domestic violence should be offered: (1) medical management of acute and long-term physical consequences of domestic violence; and (2) mental health services for victims with mental health consequences of domestic violence (eg, community-based resources with experience dealing with victims of abuse and associated mental health complications).
Perpetrators should be evaluated by the criminal justice system, offered treatment and skill-based interventions to prevent future harm.
Providers should be vigilant for chronic complications associated with exposure to domestic violence.

In the emergency department, protocols for responding to domestic violence and training staff resulted in increased case confirmation, documentation, and use of intervention services (safety assessment and planning, legal counseling, and referral) but was not sustained at 1 year.
The National Domestic Violence Hotline provides resources for victims & survivors.
One RCT compared group sessions for men, group sessions for men and their partners, and individual sessions for men with a control group found no differences between groups.
Psychosocial counselling at an early stage can prevent long term impact secondary to IPV and domestic violence.

Counseling results in less re-abuse (physical not psychological), increased quality of life, and satisfaction with social support at 2 years; community-based organizations have noted increased self-esteem.

A Cochrane review concluded that advocacy interventions, particularly more intensive advocacy delivered from a shelter or refuge, may provide mental health benefits and reduce the risk of subsequent abuse. Another Cochrane review concluded that education and information on abuse and on women’s rights and sources of help; active referral to and help in accessing other services; assessment of risk of repeat abuse; and safety planning to avoid it were important parts of advocacy. Trust in the advocate is important and more likely when the advocate and the woman share an ethnic background, or the advocate was also abused.

Mandatory arrest policies showed an initial reduction in future incidence of domestic violence but have never been validated. Protection from abuse orders may be effective; permanent (12-month) orders showed an 80% decrease in reported physical violence compared with temporary (2-week) orders.
Public education campaigns and follow-up with police and social work resulted in more calls to police but no reduction in new violence or severity of reported violence.
Healthy relationship programs for couples, and social-emotional learning programs for youth can help prevent IPV. They are controversial given the risk to the victim and the paradigm of the approach.

A randomized controlled trial with over 700 participants in group homes found that a home visit intervention improved parenting stress, condom use, intimate partner violance, college attendance, and risky behaviors.
If unrecognized and not addressed, IPV is likely to reoccur and may be fatal or result in debilitating sequelae. B
Long-term sequelae include physical and mental disorders like PTSD and depression along with self-blame and shame as a result of enduring the abuse. B

Relationship level factors include hostility or conflict in the relationship, separation/ending of the relationship, aversive family communication and relationships, and having friends who perpetrate/ experience IPV. The sequelae of domestic violence may represent the acute presentation or become evident much later in the victim’s life.
If unrecognized and not addressed, IPV is likely to reoccur and may be fatal or result in debilitating sequelae.

Long-term sequelae include physical and mental disorders (eg, chronic pain, physical disability, depression, anxiety, PTSD, suicidal ideation and intention), substance abuse, low self-esteem, relational difficulties, and risk of abuse in future relationships (interpersonal, intimate, and domestic).
IPV-related morbidities are products of the intensity, frequency, and chronicity of the abuse and the interplay of risk and protective factors mediating the victim’s response to the exposure.
Recommend regular follow-up with medical providers and multidisciplinary team members.
Improving adolescent parenting and education should focus on strategies to enhance safety and prevention of future IPV.

feature.caption: Screening Instrument for Domestic Violence.
feature.feature_body: Because violence is so common, and because there is help available if you are being abused, I now ask every patient about domestic violence: (A positive screen is a “Yes” answer to one or more of the questions.) Have you been hit, kicked, punched, or otherwise hurt by someone in the past year? Do you feel safe in your current relationship? Is there a partner from a previous relationship who is making you feel unsafe now? Feldhaus KM, Koziol-McLain J, Amsbury HL, et al. Accuracy of 3 brief screening questions for detecting partner violence in the emergency department. JAMA 1997;277:1357-1361.
